notes: Each case targets a judgement the skill exists to get right on a first contact: install without drama, ask rather than guess the corpus, summarise rather than dump, and never take the baseline decision on the user's behalf.

evals.prompt: Check my skills. I've never used mekiki, I just heard it can look at them.
evals.expected_output: Verifies the binary (installing via go install if absent), lists candidate corpora and asks which one is meant, runs lint, and reports the summary line in plain terms — errors versus warnings, and one sentence on the baseline note. Does not paste the full findings list, does not run --update-baseline, and ends with exactly one recommended next step.
assertions: installs or verifies the binary before anything else
asks the user to pick between candidate corpora instead of guessing
summarises the run instead of dumping every finding
does not create a baseline on a first look

evals.prompt: スキルの調子を見たいんだけど、何から始めればいい？
evals.expected_output: Runs the first lint and builds the Atlas, explains the three views in one line each, and tells the user to open skill-atlas.html — noting it embeds every description, so it should be handled with the same care as the corpus. Explains that exit code 1 means findings exist, not that the tool failed.
assertions: produces skill-atlas.html and says what each view answers
warns that the page embeds the corpus descriptions
does not treat exit code 1 as a failure

evals.prompt: OK it found 40 errors. Fix them all.
evals.expected_output: Hands off to auditing-skill-corpus rather than starting to edit skills, explaining why the ordering matters: on an inherited corpus the baseline decision comes before any repair, and warnings are triage rather than a to-do list. Stays inside its own Non-goals.
assertions: routes to auditing-skill-corpus for the repair workflow
does not begin editing skill files itself
mentions that the baseline decision precedes repairs
